title: Customer-facing explanation (internal draft): Auto-rollback on SLO breach for model rollouts
content:
Audience + intent
- Audience: Customer engineering leaders, platform/SRE teams, and Redwood admins evaluating or enabling rollout safety rails.
- Intent: Provide a clear explanation of what “auto-rollback on SLO breach” does, what customers will see, how configuration works, and where the boundaries are.
- Note: This is an internal draft for Solutions Eng / TAM use. Final external copy will be normalized by Product Marketing / Docs.


One-paragraph summary (recommended)
Redwood’s auto-rollback on SLO breach is a rollout safety rail that monitors latency and error-rate SLOs during a canary or A/B rollout and automatically pauses or rolls back traffic when a sustained regression is detected. Customers can scope policies per route/model/region/tier, choose conservative defaults or customize thresholds within safe bounds, and review every automated decision in the Console with an auditable “why” trail and links to the underlying metrics.


What this feature is (customer framing)
When you roll out a new model version (or change serving configuration) using Redwood Rollouts, you’re intentionally changing production traffic. Auto-rollback ties that rollout to service-level objectives (SLOs) so that if the new version causes unacceptable latency or error behavior, Redwood can automatically:
- Pause the rollout at the current step (hold steady while you investigate)
- Roll back to the last known-good model version / baseline traffic split (restore normal behavior)

This reduces time-to-mitigation during regressions, especially off-hours or under high-change velocity.


What it monitors (signals)
Auto-rollback uses SLO monitors that are eligible for rollout safety:
- Latency (p95 and/or p99) for the rollout’s exact scope
- Error rate (e.g., 5xx / request failures) for the rollout’s exact scope
- Saturation signals (where applicable) used as supporting context (not always a primary trigger in the MVP)

Important: the system evaluates SLOs in the scope of the rollout (route/service + model version + region + customer tier). This prevents a global incident or unrelated route from incorrectly impacting a targeted rollout decision.


How thresholds are chosen (how to explain defaults)
We provide safe defaults intended to catch meaningful regressions while reducing false positives:
- Two-window evaluation (fast + slow) to detect both sharp spikes and sustained degradation
- Minimum sample size gating so that very low-traffic rollouts don’t flap on noise
- Debounce/holdoff logic to prevent oscillation (e.g., repeated rollback/pause loops)

Default values vary by customer tier and service criticality (e.g., stricter for Dedicated/Private with SLAs, more conservative rollbacks for self-serve). In general:
- Higher tiers tend to use tighter error-rate triggers and stronger protections against latency regressions.
- Lower-volume routes typically require larger minimum sample thresholds or longer windows before action.

How to say it plainly:
“We use burn-rate style detection across multiple time windows, plus minimum traffic requirements. The aim is to act fast on real regressions without triggering on normal variance.”

What customers can configure:
- Whether the action is Pause-only, Rollback, or “Pause then Rollback if breach persists” (policy-dependent)
- Which SLOs are in scope (latency p95/p99, error rate)
- Threshold sensitivity within guardrails (to prevent unsafe configs)
- Suppression windows (maintenance windows, known incidents) with audit requirements


What customers will see in the Console
1) Rollout policy editor (new section)
- A dedicated “Auto-mitigation” or “SLO-based rollback” section in the rollout policy editor.
- Select a template (recommended starting point) and optionally override:
  - Breach thresholds (latency/error)
  - Evaluation windows (fast/slow)
  - Minimum sample size
  - Action type (pause vs rollback)
  - Suppression rules (who can suppress, max duration)

2) Rollout timeline / audit trail
When auto-mitigation runs, the rollout timeline shows a clear event entry, e.g.:
- “Auto-paused due to latency SLO breach”
- “Auto-rolled back due to error-rate SLO breach”
- “Auto-rollback suppressed (maintenance window)”
- “No decision: monitor missing or stale” (depending on policy)

Each event includes:
- Decision (pause / rollback / suppress / no-op)
- Scope (route, model version, region, tier)
- Which monitor(s) were evaluated
- A short explanation (“fast window breached and confirmed by slow window”, “insufficient sample size”, etc.)
- Links to dashboards/graphs for the exact scope

3) Notifications
Depending on customer setup and tier, notifications may be visible via:
- Console activity feed
- Optional Slack/email integrations (when enabled) for “auto-rollback triggered” events

We’re careful to prevent “notification storms” by grouping and rate-limiting certain notices.


What happens operationally (plain-language lifecycle)
Typical flow during a rollout:
1) You start a canary or A/B rollout for model version X.
2) The rollout controller continuously evaluates SLOs for the rollout scope.
3) If a regression is detected and confirmed (based on policy rules), Redwood automatically pauses or rolls back.
4) The rollout UI shows what happened, why it happened, and links to relevant dashboards.
5) An admin can optionally suppress auto-rollback temporarily (with justification) to continue debugging or proceed under controlled conditions.


Pause vs Rollback: how to describe the difference
- Pause: stops progressing the rollout further. Traffic stays at the current step/split. Use when you want to prevent further risk but avoid an immediate traffic shift.
- Rollback: actively shifts traffic back to baseline/previous known-good version. Use when you want immediate mitigation.

Many customers choose “pause on first breach; rollback on persistent breach” for high-sensitivity routes.


Limitations + guardrails (set expectations clearly)
This feature is intentionally conservative in the MVP and is designed as a safety rail, not a full autonomous incident responder.

Key limitations to communicate:
- Requires monitors: Auto-rollback can only act if the relevant SLO monitors exist and are healthy for that scope. Missing or stale monitors will prevent action (behavior is policy-driven).
- Not a quality guardrail: It does not evaluate output quality, correctness, toxicity, or business KPIs. (Those are handled via separate eval/guardrail systems.)
- Not full multi-region failover: It doesn’t automatically orchestrate cross-region traffic failover beyond reverting the rollout within the configured scope.
- Not a substitute for capacity planning: If a service is under-provisioned or telemetry is degraded, SLO signals may be noisy or delayed.
- Tail latency nuance: p99 can move due to batching, cache warmup, or traffic shape changes. Policies should be tuned with that in mind (we provide templates + guidance).

Safety guardrails built into the platform:
- Safe bounds on thresholds/windows (prevents extremely sensitive configs)
- Debounce/holdoff to avoid thrashing
- Minimum sample sizes to avoid acting on low-volume noise
- Audit logging for every auto-action and every suppression/override


Security, permissions, and auditability (enterprise questions)
- Every auto action is logged with a decision trace that includes: acting component, policy version, monitors evaluated, and the scope.
- Suppression/override controls are admin-only and require a justification note; these are also recorded.
- Customers can use the audit trail for compliance review and incident retrospectives.

(Internal note: Align final wording with Security review and the audit schema ADR.)


Recommended customer enablement plan (what we tell customers)
We recommend enabling auto-rollback in phases:
1) Start in staging with synthetic signal injection to validate the behavior for your route/model.
2) Enable in production for a low-risk internal route with conservative policies (pause-only).
3) Expand coverage to critical routes and add rollback behavior once monitor coverage and alert routing are validated.

Pre-req checklist (customer-friendly):
- SLO monitors exist for your route/model/region/tier
- Owners and alert routing are configured
- Your rollout policy has an approved template + tuned thresholds
- Your admins understand suppression/override controls and audit expectations


FAQ (customer-ready)
Q: Will Redwood roll back for a brief spike?
A: By default, no. We use multi-window confirmation and minimum volume checks to avoid reacting to transient blips.

Q: Can I scope this to specific regions or customer tiers?
A: Yes. Policies can be applied per route/model/region/tier so that rollouts for sensitive tenants can have stricter safety rails.

Q: What if the monitors are missing or telemetry is delayed?
A: The system will record that monitor data is missing/stale and either take no action or pause (depending on policy). We recommend gating enablement on monitor coverage.

Q: Can we override an auto-rollback?
A: Admins can suppress auto-mitigation temporarily with a required justification that’s recorded in the audit trail.

Q: Does this replace our incident response process?
A: It improves time-to-mitigation for rollout-caused regressions, but it does not replace incident response. It’s one safety rail in a broader operational toolkit.


Suggested phrasing snippets (for emails / QBRs)
- “Auto-rollback gives you a production safety rail for model rollouts: if latency or error-rate SLOs breach in a sustained way, Redwood can automatically pause or revert the rollout.”
- “Every automated decision is visible in the Console with an audit trail and a link to the relevant dashboards.”
- “You can tune thresholds and scope per region/tier, but we enforce safe bounds to reduce the chance of flapping.”


Open questions / follow-ups (internal)
- Confirm final product naming in Console: “Auto-rollback”, “Auto-mitigation”, or “SLO-based rollback”.
- Confirm external stance on missing/stale monitor behavior (policy-dependent). Ensure we don’t promise a single default behavior if it can vary.
- Confirm whether Slack notifications are GA for all tiers or only for certain plans at launch.
- Confirm what we call “last known-good” in customer copy (previous step, previous version, baseline) to avoid ambiguity.
